theory.intro: An ethical survey protects privacy, obtains consent, and ensures accessibility for all participants. Unbiased questions use neutral language with balanced, non-overlapping choices.
facts: **Informed consent** means explaining the purpose and use of responses before people agree to participate. Protect privacy by avoiding unnecessary identification and securing sensitive responses.
**Cultural responsiveness** considers different languages and cultures. Use plain language, suitable formats and choices such as 'Other' or 'Prefer not to say'.
A **leading question** uses emotive or persuasive language to prompt a specific response.
An **assumed-fact question** presumes a condition that may not apply to all respondents.
A **double-barrelled question** joins two separate topics into one question, preventing clear individual answers.
Response choices must be **balanced and exhaustive**, offering a full range of neutral options without overlapping categories.

workedExamples.question_text:
A community survey asks:
(a) 'Don't you agree that our wonderful swimming pool deserves more funding?' Identify the fault and write a neutral question.
(b) 'Should the council improve the swimming pool and build a new skate park?' Identify the fault and rewrite it.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) 'Don't you agree' and 'wonderful' suggest the answer, so this is a leading question.
A neutral question is: 'Do you support more funding for the swimming pool?' Choices: Support, Oppose, or Not sure.
(b) This combines two decisions. Someone could support one and oppose the other, so it is double-barrelled.
Ask separately: 'Do you support improving the swimming pool?' and 'Do you support building a new skate park?' Each can use Support, Oppose, or Not sure.

workedExamples.question_text:
A survey asks how many days people used the local park in the last seven days. Choices are 1–3, 3–5 or 5–7.
(a) Explain two faults and give suitable choices.
(b) Another question rates the park as Good, Very good or Excellent. Give a balanced set of choices.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) The choices overlap at 3 and 5, and leave out 0 days. The missing zero choice assumes everyone used the park.
Use 0, 1–2, 3–4 or 5–7 days. Every whole-number answer from 0 to 7 belongs to exactly one choice.
(b) All the original choices are positive. Use Very poor, Poor, Neither poor nor good, Good, or Very good. Include Have not used it for people who cannot rate it.

workedExamples.question_text:
Employees agree to give confidential feedback about their workplace. A manager puts their names beside their answers and sends the individual responses to a company that was not mentioned when the survey was explained.
(a) Identify two ethical concerns.
(b) Suggest how to collect and report this feedback responsibly.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Names identify the employees' sensitive answers, putting privacy at risk. Sending responses for an unexplained use also goes beyond the purpose participants agreed to.
(b) Explain the purpose and how answers will be used before obtaining consent. Avoid unnecessary identifying details, keep responses secure and report grouped results so individual employees are not identified. Do not share identifiable answers for another purpose without informed agreement.

workedExamples.question_text:
A neighbourhood survey is available only online, in English, with difficult technical terms. Some residents need another language or cannot use the online form.
(a) Explain the language problem and suggest a remedy.
(b) Explain the format problem and suggest a remedy.
(c) A question about religion lists only three religions. Suggest changes so more residents can answer.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Residents who cannot read the English wording well may be unable to give their views. Use plain language and provide translations suited to the community.
(b) An online-only form excludes people who cannot use it. Offer paper or phone alternatives and make the online version accessible.
(c) Add Other, No religion and Prefer not to say where appropriate. These choices recognise different beliefs and allow residents to avoid disclosing sensitive information.

foundation.question_text: A council survey asks: 'Given that trees reduce street temperatures, do you support planting more street trees?' Identify the questionnaire fault.
foundation.solution_text:
The question provides one-sided positive information before asking for an opinion.
Leading question.

foundation.question_text: A survey question asks: 'Do you agree that the council should improve parks and upgrade sports grounds?' Identify the questionnaire fault.
foundation.solution_text:
The question combines two distinct topics (parks and sports grounds) into one item.
Double-barrelled question.

foundation.question_text: A survey on commuting asks respondents: 'How many days per week do you catch the train: 1–2, 2–4, or 4–5?' Identify the questionnaire fault.
foundation.solution_text:
The options overlap at 2 and 4, and omit 0, 6 and 7 days.
Overlapping and non-exhaustive response categories.

foundation.question_text:
A medical clinic conducts a survey about patient health conditions and publishes the results online with each respondent's full name and address.
Identify the ethical principle violated.
foundation.solution_text:
Publishing health conditions with names and addresses reveals sensitive personal information.
This breaches privacy and confidentiality. Publish grouped results without identifying respondents.

foundation.question_text:
A community survey about public services is printed only in English in a suburb where $60\%$ of residents speak Arabic as their primary language.
State the diversity issue and how to resolve it.
foundation.solution_text:
English-only wording may exclude residents who cannot read English well; speaking Arabic as a primary language does not itself mean someone cannot read English.
Provide Arabic translations and plain-language English so more residents can respond.

foundation.question_text: A survey asks: 'How terrible was your experience with our competitor's customer service?' Identify the dominant fault and rewrite the question neutrally.
foundation.solution_text:
The word 'terrible' suggests a negative answer, so the question is leading.
Rewrite: 'How would you rate your experience with our competitor's customer service?'
Choices: Very poor, Poor, Neither poor nor good, Good, Very good, or Have not used it.

foundation.question_text:
A researcher surveys high school students about illegal substance use and tells them participation is compulsory.
Identify the ethical issue.
foundation.solution_text:
Compulsory participation pressures students to disclose sensitive information in this research survey.
Explain its purpose and how responses will be used, seek informed consent, and allow students to decline or skip sensitive questions.

development.question_text:
A school survey asks: 'How many days did you ride your bicycle to school last school week: 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5?'
Identify the fault and rewrite it so it is fair to all students.
development.solution_text:
The choices assume every student rode a bicycle at least once. Students who did not ride have no answer.
Rewrite: 'How many days did you ride a bicycle to school last school week: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5?'

development.question_text:
A transport survey asks respondents to rate a new bus route using the choices: 'Acceptable', 'Good', 'Very Good', and 'Outstanding'.
Explain why this set of response options is biased.
development.solution_text:
All choices are positive or neutral, with no negative options available for dissatisfied riders.
Unbalanced response choices.

development.question_text:
An online shopping website secretly collects browsing data from users without their knowledge or consent to create customer profiles.
Identify the ethical violation and explain why it is unacceptable.
development.solution_text:
Data was collected without informing participants or obtaining permission.
Violation of informed consent and transparent data collection.

development.question_text:
A demographic survey asking about religion includes only Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism, with no 'Other' or 'No religion' option.
Explain why this design is flawed and how to fix it.
development.solution_text:
The options exclude individuals of other faiths or no faith.
Include 'Other (please specify)', 'No religion', and 'Prefer not to say'.

development.question_text: A questionnaire asks: 'Should the government reduce taxes and increase spending on hospitals?' Explain why this question is flawed and provide a two-question rewrite.
development.solution_text:
It is a double-barrelled question asking about two separate fiscal policies at once.
Rewrite: '1. Should the government reduce taxes?' and '2. Should the government increase spending on hospitals?'

development.question_text:
A workplace survey collects employee opinions on executive management performance.
Employees are required to write their employee payroll ID on the form.
Explain why this design compromises survey validity.
development.solution_text:
Requiring payroll IDs removes anonymity, which may lead employees to give dishonest responses due to fear of repercussions.
Lack of participant anonymity.

development.question_text: A café survey asks: 'Do you agree that our freshly baked artisan bread is delicious?' Rewrite the question neutrally with a balanced set of response options.
development.solution_text:
The question uses leading, emotive adjectives ('freshly baked artisan', 'delicious').
Rewrite: 'How would you rate the quality of the bread: Very poor, Poor, Neutral, Good, Excellent, or Have not tried it?'

mastery.question_text:
A university researcher collects genetic data from participants for an allergy study.
The researcher later sells this identifiable personal data to private insurance companies without participant knowledge.
Identify two major ethical violations committed.
mastery.solution_text:
1. Violation of informed consent (participants consented only to an allergy study, not commercial sale).
2. Breach of privacy and secure data handling (identifiable sensitive data shared with third parties).

mastery.question_text: A council feedback form on library renovations asks: 'Given that modern digital resources are essential for children's education, don't you agree that spending \$2 million on computers is a fantastic investment?' Identify two questionnaire faults and write a single, neutral, objective question to gauge resident support.
mastery.solution_text:
The question provides one-sided leading context and uses emotive language ('essential', 'fantastic').
Rewrite: 'Do you support spending \$2 million on library computers: Strongly oppose, Oppose, Neutral, Support, or Strongly support?'

mastery.question_text:
A national health survey on mental wellbeing is administered only as a fast-paced online form with complex technical jargon, requiring facial recognition verification.
Explain two ways this survey fails accessibility and ethical standards, and propose specific remedies.
mastery.solution_text:
1. Complex jargon, a fast pace and an online-only form may prevent people with reading difficulties, visual impairments or limited digital access from responding. Provide plain-language text, enough time, screen-reader support and paper or phone alternatives.
2. Facial scanning collects unnecessary identifying information for this sensitive survey. Remove the scan and avoid collecting identifying details that are not needed.
